items.title: AI‐Supported Research‐Led Teaching in Syntegrative Project‐Based Learning: Educator Questioning, Feedback, and Student Learning Outcomes in Authentic Industry Projects
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for connecting research‐led teaching with authentic industry projects, yet its educational value depends on how educators organize inquiry rather than on technological use alone. This study examined the relationships among AI‐supported research‐led teaching (AIRLT), educator questioning (EQ), educator feedback (EF), student inquiry engagement (SIE), and authentic project learning outcomes (APLO) within Syntegrative Project‐Based Learning. A quantitative cross‐sectional survey was conducted with 898 undergraduate students from 12 universities in Vietnam who had participated in authentic industry or organizational projects involving AI‐supported inquiry and educator guidance. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) showed that AIRLT was positively associated with EQ ( β = 0.642) and EF ( β = 0.611). Both EQ ( β = 0.463) and EF ( β = 0.349) were positively associated with SIE, which, in turn, showed a strong positive association with APLO ( β = 0.689). All six specific indirect effects were significant, indicating statistically significant indirect associations among AI‐supported teaching, educator guidance, student inquiry, and perceived authentic learning outcomes. The findings contribute an educator‐mediated perspective to Syntegrative Education by showing that AI is most educationally meaningful when embedded in purposeful questioning, feedback, and sustained student inquiry. The study highlights the importance of designing AI‐supported industry projects around evidence evaluation, iterative feedback, reflection, and active investigation of authentic problems rather than treating AI use as an educational objective in itself.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Professional Transformation: A Comparative Study of Legal and Accounting Professionals in Mumbai
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming professional services through automation, information processing, analytics and decision support. Legal and accounting professions, which rely on expertise, judgment, confidentiality and compliance, are increasingly exposed to AI technologies, though adoption and perceived impacts may differ between the two fields. This study examines and compares AI adoption and professional transformation among legal and accounting professionals in Mumbai. It focuses on AI awareness, adoption, perceived benefits, professional transformation, ethical concerns, skills, employment implications and future adoption intentions. A quantitative research design using a structured questionnaire will be adopted, with data analysed through descriptive, reliability, correlation and comparative statistical techniques. The study aims to identify similarities, differences and factors influencing AI adoption, providing insights for effective AI training, governance and responsible adoption. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI Adoption, Legal Professionals, Accounting Professionals, Professional Transformation, Technology Adoption, Mumbai

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications for Early Disease Detection in Healthcare Systems
items.abstract: With delayed access to specialist expertise and subjective interpretation by clinicians and workload limiting the ability to access parts of the pathway, early disease detection is one of the most impactful levers that can be used to improve patient outcomes and reduce the cost of care.Medical image analysis, electronic health records (EHR), genomic data analysis, and analysis of physiological signals are all examples of medical data that can be transformed by artificial intelligence (AI) and especially machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), as there is no way they could be analyzed at the same scale and speed as would be possible by a human being.In this paper we bring together existing evidence of the use of AI in early detection in oncology, cardiology, neurology, dermatology, ophthalmology and critical care.It discusses the mathematical approaches used for their analysis such as the use of convolutional neural networks for image analysis and recurrent networks for time-series analysis of physiological data, and compares their reported diagnostic performance with that of conventional clinical analyses.The paper also examines real-world challenges to adoption, such as standardization of data, algorithmic bias, regulatory approval processes and clinician acceptance, and proposes some solutions.The results suggest that AI systems perform as well as or better than humans in precisely defined detection tasks but will not automatically translate this to better population health outcomes without attention to data quality, the need to integrate AI systems into workflows, and the need to ensure that everyone has access to them.The paper ends with policy, research and system recommendations for maximizing early detection programmatic value while responsibly scaling these initiatives.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as an Organizational Actor: Transforming Power, Authority, and Responsibility
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in organizations is transforming organizational roles, relationships, and balances of power and authority. This chapter examines how AI can be positioned not merely as a traditional technological tool, but as an organizational actor that participates in decision-making, knowledge production, coordination, and action processes. This transformation necessitates the redefinition of employees’ roles and the reconfiguration of collaborative relationships between humans and AI. The chapter first evaluates the opportunities offered by AI to organizations, along with its potential key risks. It then examines the evolving role of AI, from a tool to an assistant and subsequently to a team member/business partner, and discusses the organizational implications of human-AI collaboration. In particular, the increasing integration of AI into organizational processes is examined in terms of power, control, authority, responsibility, and accountability relationships. Finally, employees’ perceptions of AI are addressed, emphasizing the importance of organizational acceptance. In summary, this chapter examines the transformation of AI’s role in organizations and human-AI interaction, with a particular focus on the implications of this transformation for organizational processes, employees, and organizational structures.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Development and Worker Employment Quality: Evidence from China
items.abstract: With the continuous development of new technologies, these new technologies have a profound impact on the labor market. This paper uses micro-individual data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) from 2016 to 2022 and provincial-level macro-data on artificial intelligence (AI), employing a two-way fixed-effects model to systematically examine the actual impact and underlying mechanisms of AI development on the employment quality of workers. The study shows a significant positive correlation between the level of regional artificial intelligence development and the employment quality of local workers. However, this overall effect at the regional level cannot directly prove the individual-level effect of enterprises or employees using artificial intelligence. Mechanism testing further confirms that the effect of the regional AI development on improving the employment quality of workers is mainly achieved through optimizing the industrial structure and promoting the intelligentization of workers’ working mode. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the regional artificial intelligence has a greater positive impact on employment quality for male workers, outside-system workers, and workers in the eastern region. Therefore, to achieve higher-quality employment for workers, it is necessary to promote the deep integration of AI with the real economy, build a multi-party collaborative education mechanism involving government, enterprises, and universities, and implement policies to promote digital inclusion and differentiated support.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Smart Grid and Renewable Energy Management: A Review of Techniques, Applications, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Intermittent renewable generation, volatile loads, and concerns over grid stability have become defining features of modern power systems. Addressing these challenges with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) is attracting growing attention, including through better forecasting, automated demand response, optimized energy storage, and smart grid fault detection. This paper highlights the various AI-based techniques developed across the smart grid landscape, ranging from solar and wind forecasting to short-term load forecasting, demand-side management, electricity price forecasting, energy storage and battery management, grid resilience, and digital twins. It offers an overview of recently published work, including the major approaches, namely deep learning (LSTM and Transformer models), explainable AI, multi-agent systems, reinforcement learning, and federated learning, together with their strengths and limitations. The paper also presents a conceptual three-layer framework comprising edge sensing, federated forecasting and control, and explainable operator support at the distribution-utility level; the framework is not validated empirically. Challenges such as data privacy, model interpretability, scalability, and cybersecurity are explored, together with future research directions and the relevance of these technologies to India’s energy transition goals.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Era of Globalisation: Implications for Students’ Attitudes, Socialization and Career Perspectives in India
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant component of the contemporary globalised world, influencing education, communication, employment, and daily social interactions. Its growing presence in higher education is transforming how students gather information, complete academic tasks, communicate with others, and prepare for their careers. This article analyses the impact of AI on students' attitudes, socialisation, and professional perspectives, particularly within the Indian context. The study employs a qualitative methodology based on secondary data, using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, government policy documents, and reports from recognised national and international institutions. The analysis shows that while students generally acknowledge AI's educational value, factors such as institutional support, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, and trust in AI-generated information shape their attitudes. Although AI can facilitate learning and collaborative educational activities, overreliance on it—at the expense of human interaction—may raise concerns about social engagement and interpersonal relationships. Regarding employment, AI is simultaneously transforming existing professions, creating new job opportunities, and altering the skill sets expected of graduates. According to the World Economic Forum, the transformation of the labour market by 2030 could lead to the creation of 170 million new jobs and the displacement of 90 million, resulting in a net increase of 78 million jobs. India is addressing these changes through initiatives such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, India AI FutureSkills, and NITI Aayog’s roadmap for job creation in the AI economy. The article represents the acceptance of a human-oriented model for mixing AI into Indian higher education—one that coordinates technical expertise with critical thinking, academic honesty, social involvement, employability, and moral accountability.

items.title: Artificial intelligence–enabled nursing surveillance for pediatric cancer immunotherapy: integrating biomarkers, patient-reported outcomes, and long-term toxicity management
items.abstract: Pediatric cancer immunotherapy has expanded from anti-GD2 antibodies and bispecific T-cell engagers to immune checkpoint inhibitors and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy. These treatments can produce rapid, nonlinear, and partially overlapping toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, infection, prolonged cytopenia, B-cell aplasia, and organ-specific immune-related adverse events. Nurses provide the highest-frequency clinical observations across inpatient, ambulatory, and home settings, yet conventional monitoring often fragments laboratory data, vital signs, neurologic findings, caregiver observations, and patient-reported outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a means to fuse these longitudinal signals into individualized risk trajectories. The clinically relevant mechanism, however, is not autonomous prediction; it is a nurse-in-the-loop system in which AI improves temporal sensitivity and prioritization, while nurses verify signal quality, interpret age- and development-specific context, reconcile child–caregiver discordance, activate protocol-based escalation, and maintain accountability. This Mini Review examines how biomarkers, continuous physiological monitoring, electronic patient-reported outcomes, and caregiver-reported behavioral changes can support AI-enabled nursing surveillance during acute immunotoxicity and long-term survivorship. We propose a three-layer framework linking immune-toxicity biology, a multimodal digital phenotype, and nursing counter-regulation. We also discuss workflow integration, alert fatigue, model drift, bias, privacy, and the need for prospective pediatric validation. AI should augment not replace specialist pediatric oncology nursing judgment and should be evaluated by whether it improves timely intervention, symptom burden, family experience, and long-term safety.

items.title: Attitudes and perceptions toward artificial intelligence among practicing rheumatologists in Iraq: a cross-sectional web-based survey
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of healthcare, particularly in rheumatology, where clinicians must integrate complex clinical, laboratory, and imaging data. Physicians’ perceptions of AI may substantially influence the extent to which it is implemented responsibly in routine clinical practice. Objective This study aimed to assess the attitudes of practicing rheumatologists in Iraq toward artificial intelligence and to examine their association with demographic and professional characteristics. Methods A four-month web-based cross-sectional survey was conducted from October 2025 to January 2026. A questionnaire adapted from previous studies was refined through expert review and pilot testing before distribution. The questionnaire comprised demographic information, attitude statements measured on a five-point Likert scale, and items assessing general perceptions of artificial intelligence. Composite attitude scores were categorized using modified Bloom's cutoff criteria. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS and R. Results A total of 162 complete responses were collected. Most respondents were aged 35–44 years (42.0%), male (56.8%), and specialists (67.9%). Overall, 61.7% reported familiarity with AI and 69.1% had already used AI in rheumatology practice. Most participants 56.8% exhibited a poor attitude, 32.1% a moderate attitude, and 11.1% a good attitude toward AI. Bivariate analysis identified familiarity with AI ( p = 0.003 ) and involvement in research ( p = 0.009 ) as significantly associated with more favorable attitudes. Conclusion Iraqi rheumatologists demonstrate cautious engagement with artificial intelligence, with the majority displaying poor-to-moderate overall attitude scores on the standardized composite scale. Greater familiarity with AI and research involvement were associated with more favorable attitudes, highlighting the importance of targeted digital literacy and specialty-specific education to support effective AI adoption in clinical practice.

items.title: Autonomous agents and multi-agent systems: a comprehensive review
items.abstract: Autonomous agents and multi-agent systems have rapidly advanced with the integration of large language models (LLMs), enabling increasingly capable reasoning, planning, tool use, and collaboration. However, the field remains fragmented by inconsistent architectural terminology, limited cross-domain comparison, and heterogeneous evaluation practices. This review addresses these gaps through a two-stage PRISMA-informed search combining Scopus with structured manual screening, covering 107 peer-reviewed original studies published between 2018 and 2026. We propose a unified five-module architecture comprising profile, memory, planning, action, and security; systematically compare agent capabilities across ten application domains; and organize evaluation practices into six dimensions: task performance, efficiency, quality, robustness, safety, and interpretability. The review identifies two recurring patterns across domains: explicit integration of domain knowledge consistently improves performance, while planner–executor–reflector role specialization appears across diverse applications. However, technical performance often exceeds validated real-world utility, with robustness, safety, and interpretability remaining particularly under-evaluated. These findings provide a common basis for understanding, comparing, and developing autonomous agents and highlight priorities for more reliable and practically deployable systems.

items.title: Beyond AI Tutors: A Human-Centred Framework for Goal-Driven Learning Agents in Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing education by offering new ways to explain concepts, support teachers, and personalise student learning. However, many conventional educational chatbots focus on answering individual questions rather than coordinating the complete learning process. Students often need more than an answer: they need a learning plan, suitable practice activities, feedback on mistakes, and guidance about what to study next. Agentic artificial intelligence offers a possible way to coordinate these activities around a defined learning objective. This paper reviews selected research published between 2024 and 2026 on pedagogical AI agents, large language model agents, and agentic systems in education. The reviewed literature highlights opportunities for personalized tutoring, adaptive feedback, assignment support, and teacher assistance. It also identifies concerns involving inaccurate outputs, student dependency, privacy, fairness, accountability, and limited real-world evaluation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a human-centred framework that connects learning-goal identification, task planning, trusted educational resources, instructional support, progress evaluation, and adaptive follow-up. The framework centres student independence, teacher judgement, and responsible data use. It is a conceptual proposal and has not yet been experimentally evaluated. Future research should assess its educational effectiveness, reliability, accessibility, and suitability for different learning environments

items.title: Beyond AI Use: How AI Literacy Is Linked to Critical Thinking through AI-Assisted Problem-Solving Ability and AI Reliance
items.abstract: With the widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, helping learners use AI effectively to solve language-related problems while maintaining independent judgment and critical thinking has become a key issue in technologyenhanced language education. However, existing studies have largely focused on EFL learners’ acceptance of AI, intentions to use it, and usage behaviors, offering limited explanations of how AI literacy shapes learners’ interactions with AI and relates to critical thinking. To address this gap, the present study drew on self-regulated learning theory and adopted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Questionnaire data from 450 university students with generative AIassisted EFL learning experience were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Subsequently, 20 participants selected through stratified purposive sampling took part in semi-structured interviews, which were analyzed thematically. Quantitative results showed that AI literacy was positively associated with AI-assisted problem-solving ability and indirectly associated with critical thinking through AI-assisted problem-solving ability and AI reliance. Thematic analysis further revealed how learners translated AI-related knowledge and skills into effective problem-solving practices and how different levels of cognitive control were associated with distinct patterns of AI use and cognitive outcomes. This study deepens the understanding of the internal cognitive mechanisms underlying EFL learners’ adaptation to AI and provides practical implications for the systematic development of AI literacy and critical thinking in EFL education.

items.title: Beyond Automation: Towards Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming Human Resource Management (HRM) across the employee lifecycle, including recruitment, selection, learning and development, performance management, employee engagement, workforce planning, and talent retention. Existing discussions frequently emphasize the capacity of AI to automate repetitive activities, improve efficiency, process large volumes of data, and support predictive decision-making. However, the increasing use of algorithmic systems in decisions affecting employees also raises fundamental concerns regarding privacy, bias, transparency, accountability, employee trust, and the potential erosion of human interaction within organizations. This creates an important paradox: technologies introduced to improve HR efficiency may either strengthen or weaken the humancentered nature of HRM. This study examines the question: Can Artificial Intelligence make Human Resource Management more human? The paper adopts an analytical and conceptual research approach based on existing academic literature, institutional publications, and contemporary evidence concerning AI and the future of work. Rather than viewing AI as either a replacement for HR professionals or merely an efficiency-enhancing technology, the study investigates the conditions under which AI can support meaningful human–technology collaboration .The analysis proposes the Human-Centered AI Trust Framework, which argues that the effectiveness of AI-powered HR depends on the interaction between technological capability and five critical governance dimensions: transparency, fairness, privacy, human oversight, and employee trust. The study argues that AI does not inherently humanize or dehumanize HR. Automation can free HR professionals from repetitive administrative activities and create greater capacity for employee interaction, empathy, relationship management, and strategic work. Conversely, poorly governed AI can increase surveillance, reduce trust, reproduce bias, and create impersonal workplaces. The paper concludes that the future of HR should not be understood as a competition between Artificial Intelligence and Human Intelligence. Instead, sustainable HR transformation requires AI systems to be governed by human judgment, ethical responsibility, and employee-centered values. The most successful organizations may therefore be those that use AI not to remove humans from HR, but to enable humans to perform the aspects of HR that require them to be most human.

items.title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability
items.abstract: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. This paper introduces the Mental World Model (MWM) and its implementation, the Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA), which explicitly constructs subjective worlds, models interactions between cognition and mental states, and simulates continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences. On DynToM and RecToM, MMEA achieves 96.48% and 94.00% accuracy, respectively, outperforming leading LLMs and specialized ToM methods. Additional experiments demonstrate improvements of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental state inference, respectively. The results demonstrate that MMEA provides an interpretable framework for continuous mental modeling, enabling AI to move beyond surface-level semantic representations to infer individuals' underlying mental states from linguistic information and dynamically simulate their internal cognitive processes and evolution over time. MWM also provides a promising foundation for causal reasoning, personalized AI, sustained human-AI interaction, and future advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

items.title: Beyond Points and Badges: How Mobile-Based Gamification Drives Multidimensional Engagement to Improve Learning Outcomes in Engineering Education
items.abstract: Gamification and mobile-based learning have become popular innovative approaches in education. However, empirical evidence regarding their effectiveness in engineering education, particularly in electrical engineering, remains fragmented, with a critical gap in understanding the mediating mechanisms through which gamification drives outcomes in this uniquely demanding context. This study examines the impact of mobile-based gamification (MobGam) on learning engagement (LE) and learning outcomes (LO) among electrical engineering students. Research data were collected through standardized questionnaires from 121 students and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that the Usage Intensity of MobGam (UI) has a positive and significant effect on all dimensions of students’ LE, namely Behavioral Engagement (BE), Cognitive Engagement (CE), and Emotional Engagement (EE). UI also positively associated with LO, as measured by perceived learning effectiveness (PLE) and perceived academic performance (PAP). Moreover, LE mediates the relationship between UI and LO. Crucially, EE emerged as the strongest mediating pathway, underscoring the paramount importance of affective factors in overcoming the cognitive demands of engineering coursework. Specifically, EE showed the most substantial mediating effect on PLE (β = 0.326) and PAP (β = 0.314). These findings extend beyond electrical engineering education by providing evidence that emotionally resonant gamification is associated with higher persistence and more positive perceived LO, particularly in contexts with high cognitive load. This study offers a theoretically grounded, empirically validated model that redefines the success of educational gamification in electrical engineering education, shifting focus from mere usage to the cultivation of deep, emotionally resonant engagement.

items.title: Building Bots That Teach Thinking: Using Custom AI Chatbots to Enhance Critical Thinking and Decision-Making
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly common in education, but its effect on student learning depends largely on how it is used. This interactive session will introduce practical strategies for creating custom AI chatbots that encourage students to think through problems rather than simply ask for answers. Participants will explore ways to design bots that ask learners to explain their reasoning, consider alternative perspectives, identify assumptions, and revise their thinking before receiving feedback. Examples from healthcare education and other disciplines will show how these tools can support guided inquiry, reflective questioning, clinical reasoning, and decision-making. Participants will review and revise sample chatbot instructions, then begin developing a bot for a course or learning activity of their choice. The session will also cover practical considerations such as choosing reliable source materials, setting appropriate boundaries, protecting student privacy, testing the bot before use, and refining instructions based on its responses. Participants will leave with sample prompts, practical design principles, and a plan for using a custom chatbot in their own educational setting. The goal is to help educators use AI in ways that preserve productive struggle, provide a safe environment for practice, and strengthen students’ ability to explain and defend their decisions.

items.title: ChatGPT Awareness and Utilization Among Undergraduate Biology Education Students at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka: Implications for Mathematics Education
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has created new opportunities for learning while also raising concerns about accuracy, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on automated outputs. This study examined awareness, utilization, challenges, and perceived institutional responses to ChatGPT among undergraduate Biology Education students at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. A descriptive survey design was adopted. Eighty questionnaires were distributed to students across 100–400 levels, and 67 usable responses were returned, representing an 83.75% response rate. Data were collected using a researcher-developed Questionnaire on the Extent of Awareness and Usage of ChatGPT (QEAUC), which demonstrated an overall Cronbach’s alpha of .798. Frequency and percentage were used to analyse awareness items, while mean and standard deviation were used for utilization, challenges, and proposed solutions. The findings showed substantial awareness of ChatGPT: respondents demonstrated awareness on seven of eight awareness items, although only 25.4% recognized that ChatGPT uses natural language processing to understand and respond to queries. Overall utilization was high (M = 2.81, SD = 0.81 on a 4-point scale), with particularly high use for content creation, academic research, education, assignments, brainstorming, and conversation practice. Respondents also agreed that important barriers included inadequate internet access (M = 3.64), training costs (M = 3.46), and rote or superficial use (M = 3.51). The strongest proposed solutions were free internet access (M = 3.85), free Wi-Fi (M = 3.82), curriculum integration (M = 3.76), and guided learning activities (M = 3.58). The study concludes that ChatGPT is already embedded in the academic practices of many participating Biology Education students, but effective integration requires AI literacy, reliable digital infrastructure, explicit institutional guidance, and assessment practices that preserve student thinking and academic integrity.

items.title: Cognitive Engagement, Learning Strategies, Adjustment to College and Academic Motivation: A Structural Equation Model on Academic Success Among College Students
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.

items.title: Concept before capability - a validity-led approach to AI in OSCEs
items.abstract: Abstract Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) remain central to the assessment of clinical competence, yet the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into assessment design, delivery, and scoring raises a fundamental question: what evidence of competence are OSCEs intended to generate? This paper argues that AI should be evaluated through the lens of OSCE validity, with particular attention to how it may strengthen or weaken the interpretive chain linking observed performance to assessment decisions. Drawing on Messick’s unitary conception of validity and Kane’s argument-based framework, we examine how AI may introduce distinct threats across the scoring, generalisation, extrapolation, and implication inferences that underpin OSCE interpretation. We argue that generative AI (genAI) creates a particular risk of construct drift, whereby plausible assessment materials or scoring processes gradually reward observable proxies rather than the underlying clinical capabilities they are intended to assess. To translate this validity perspective into practice, we propose a framework that maps AI applications across the OSCE workflow according to their proximity to candidate consequences and the evidential burden required to justify their use. Lower-risk applications, such as design support and post-hoc analytics, may strengthen assessment when accompanied by construct-focused review and human oversight, whereas higher-risk uses, including AI-mediated candidate encounters and automated summative scoring, require substantially stronger validity evidence. We conclude that AI should be adopted according to the principle of concept before capability: assessment communities must first establish what clinical competence means and what evidence should count before deciding where AI has a legitimate role in high-stakes assessment.

items.title: Conceptualising Digital Transformation Through Recursive Capability Constriction: Evidence from Australian NDIS Providers
items.abstract: Digital transformation is a strategic priority across care-intensive service sectors, yet many organisations struggle to realise its intended benefits. Existing research often examines technological, organisational, and environmental barriers separately, offering limited insight into their interconnections within organisational systems. Drawing on Systems Theory and Sociotechnical Systems (STS) Theory, this study investigates digital transformation among small and medium providers within Australia’s National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Using an interpretive qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 participants from 15 distinct NDIS provider organisations in Sydney, Australia, followed by reflexive thematic analysis and systems-oriented interpretation. Participants described recurring associations among technological misalignment, fragmented software, adaptive workarounds, increased administrative demands, and constraints on organisational capacity for digital improvement, with regulatory and resource pressures interacting with these technological and organisational conditions. Building on these cross-sectional patterns, this study develops Recursive Capability Constriction (RCC), a systems-based conceptual framework that proposes how technological misalignment, compensatory adaptation, administrative expansion, and constrained organisational capability for digital improvement may become interconnected through reinforcing relationships. Rather than representing an inevitable or empirically established causal sequence, RCC provides a conditional explanation of how local adaptations may become associated with constraints on subsequent digital improvement. items.title: Corporate ethical and responsible AI (CERAi) and AI trustworthiness: a lifecycle perspective and empirical insights
items.abstract: Purpose This study develops and empirically validates a Corporate Ethical and Responsible AI (CERAi) lifecycle framework. The framework comprises three interdependent stages: design and development, testing and training, and deployment and usage. The study aims to move the research beyond abstract principles and policy analyses toward empirically grounded, lifecycle-integrated artificial intelligence AI governance theory. It positions ethical AI and responsible AI governance as the two constitutive components of the CERAi construct, and AI trustworthiness as a conceptually and empirically distinct downstream outcome anchored in stage-specific organizational governance mechanisms. The CERAi framework is scoped broadly to encompass governance of both conventional/traditional machine learning models and autonomous AI agents operating within organizational settings. Design/methodology/approach We administered a large-scale survey to 500 attendees at a national AI conference in the United States in early 2026, yielding 143 useable responses from AI professionals across healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, retail and energy sectors. We developed and validated multi-item scales for each CERAi lifecycle stage using established ethical AI and AI governance frameworks. Structural equation modeling was employed to assess the measurement model and to test both direct path hypotheses and mediation hypotheses. Findings Both CERAIi design and development and CERAi deployment and usage have significant positive direct effects on AI trustworthiness, whereas CERAi testing and training do not. Our results also indicate a significant serial mediation pathway in which CERAi deployment and usage enhance AI trustworthiness through testing and training, followed by design and development. Conversely, testing and training alone do not mediate the relationship between deployment and usage and AI trustworthiness, indicating that design-stage ethics serve as an intervening (mediating) mechanism through which governance activity enacted at later lifecycle stages is associated with perceived AI trustworthiness. This is consistent with testing and training's association with trustworthiness operating indirectly, mediated by the ethical architecture established during the design and development stage. Originality/value Findings of this study demonstrate that AI trustworthiness reflects differentiated perceived salience across AI lifecycle stages, whereby stakeholders appear to weight visible, deployment-stage governance more heavily than upstream design and testing stage governance in forming trustworthiness judgments, rather than reflecting a definitive validation that governance effects accumulate uniformly across all stages in isolation. This study makes a distinctive contribution by providing empirical evidence for a governance-sequencing mechanism, whereby design-stage ethics function as a mediating pathway shaping the effectiveness of governance activity at later lifecycle stages. To the best of our knowledge, such a mediated, stage-sequential mechanism has not previously been demonstrated using primary data within a comprehensive, three-stage CERAi lifecycle framework linking organizational ethical and responsible governance practices to AI trustworthiness outcomes.

items.title: Design Thinking for Mathematical Critical Thinking in Digital Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Mathematical critical thinking in digital learning requires purposeful interaction among pedagogical tasks, digital tools, and students' interpretation and justification of mathematical ideas. This systematic literature review examines the complementary functions of GeoGebra, Problem-Based Learning (PBL), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Meaningful Learning, and Design Thinking. The manuscript reports a qualitative thematic synthesis of 15 primary empirical studies published within the 2020–2026 search period and identified through Scopus, ERIC, Google Scholar, DOAJ, and Garuda. The available reporting record does not preserve complete database-specific retrieval and screening counts or item-level methodological appraisal results; the review therefore does not claim a fully reproducible PRISMA 2020 selection record. Across the cited evidence, GeoGebra provides dynamic mathematical representations; PBL structures problem-centred inquiry; AI offers feedback and alternative approaches that require mathematical verification; and Meaningful Learning emphasizes connections with prior knowledge. Design Thinking is proposed as a learner-centred organizing process through Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test. These differentiated functions support a conceptually coherent, potentially testable instructional pathway rather than a demonstrated effect of the combined intervention. Future research should verify the primary-study corpus, document review procedures in full, and test the proposed relationships in classroom settings.

items.title: Designing an AI Agent That Does Not Tutor: Design Rules for Socratic Probing in Introductory Physics
items.abstract: Instructors need to know whether a student understands a concept, not only whether the student can produce a correct answer, and the two have come apart: a student can paste a physics question into a chatbot and submit a fluent, correct answer without understanding it. We built a conversational AI agent for introductory mechanics that only probes. It is designed as an instrument that a correct answer alone should not pass. Its key measure is cave detection: identifying a correct first idea that the student abandons when a single variable of the scenario is changed. A single right-or-wrong item cannot see this. The agent asks a student to commit to a prediction about an everyday situation, explain it without physics vocabulary, and defend that explanation against a changed case built from the student's own words. It does not teach, hint, confirm, or correct, and it reports nothing until the end. Such an instrument works only if its replies give nothing away. LLM agents tend to leak evaluation: praise, word choice, reply length, and pacing reveal whether an answer was right, and a student who knows stops reasoning. We report design rules that suppress this leakage, derived from eight versions of the agent and more than 40 scripted simulation runs. The obvious fixes often made leakage worse: listing forbidden praise phrases increased praise, and a single worked example in the prompt spread into unrelated conversations. Each changed case had to alter exactly one variable; otherwise a changed answer could not be traced to a single idea. The evidence is simulation evidence only: no real students have used the agent, and the author wrote both the personas and the scoring rules. This paper reports design findings, not learning outcomes.

items.title: Designing Human-AI Collaborative Science: The 9A Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for Science is often described as a progression from human-directed assistance toward increasingly autonomous AI scientists. Human-AI collaboration offers a further mode in which human and AI contributions substantively shape scientific reasoning, judgments, and the course of inquiry. Existing research addresses work allocation, human-AI coordination, and system evaluation, but how these aspects interact to shape collaborative scientific systems remains insufficiently articulated. We develop the 9A Framework for Human-AI Collaborative Science (HACS) to connect these considerations across three layers. The organization layer specifies what scientific activities are required (Activity), who performs them (Actor), and who holds authority over consequential decisions (Authority). The coordination layer addresses how participants access relevant research information (Awareness), how scientific work advances through iterative proposal, execution, examination, revision, and resolution (Accountability), and when collaborative arrangements should be adjusted (Adaptability). The evaluation layer establishes what constitutes effective system performance (Achievement), how comparisons can be designed to identify the effects of organizational and coordination choices (Attribution), and what evidence supports the resulting conclusions (Assurance). Together, these layers frame HACS as a system-design problem, providing a basis for designing collaborative scientific workflows and for empirically comparing their effectiveness.

items.title: Designing Teaching Materials with GenAI: Perceptions of Cognitive Load and Learner Competencies in Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to design instructional materials in higher education, yet limited evidence exists on students’ perceptions of the cognitive demands and learner-related competencies involved. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, this study examined university students’ perceptions of GenAI-supported instructional material design according to gender, age, and admission grade. A quantitative, non-experimental, ex post facto study was conducted with 451 university students enrolled in education-related undergraduate and master’s programmes. The instrument assessed perceived usefulness, beliefs concerning metacognitive practices, prior knowledge, and problem-solving strategies, and perceived intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load. Participants generally reported positive perceptions. Female students reported significantly higher scores on the metacognitive skills, prior knowledge, and problem-solving skills dimensions, although effect sizes were small. These differences should be interpreted cautiously, given that female students represented 82% of the sample. No statistically significant gender differences were detected in the cognitive load dimensions. Age showed only a weak negative association with extraneous cognitive load, whereas admission grade was positively associated with metacognitive scores in both gender groups and with prior knowledge and problem-solving scores among female students. The findings describe students’ beliefs about the practices and cognitive demands associated with GenAI-supported material design and may inform training in the critical review and pedagogical adaptation of AI-generated teaching materials.

items.title: Development and Evaluation of AI-Integrated Digital Learning Modules for Food and Beverage Operations Under the Strengthened Senior High School Tech-Pro Curriculum
items.abstract: This study developed and evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated digital learning modules for Food and Beverage Operations under the Strengthened Senior High School Tech-Pro Curriculum. Using a developmental-descriptive research design with a one-group pretest–posttest quasi-experimental component, it involved 84 Grade 11 learners and five TLE/TVL teachers from five public secondary schools in Agusan del Sur, together with three expert validators. The modules were examined in terms of instructional features, competency alignment, validity, and acceptability. Expert evaluation questionnaires, teacher and student acceptability questionnaires, and achievement tests supplied the data, which were analyzed using means, standard deviations, mean percentage scores, independent-samples t-tests, and a paired-samples t-test. The six instructional feature dimensions were rated highly evident (means = 4.60–4.80), and the five validity dimensions were assessed as highly valid (means = 4.67–4.80). Teachers and students considered the modules highly acceptable, with no statistically significant differences in their ratings across the five dimensions (all p > .05). The reported mean percentage score rose from 69.4 on the pretest to 78.0 on the posttest. The paired comparison of achievement-test scores was statistically significant (t = −11.303, p < .001). The findings support the modules’ suitability as supplementary, competency-aligned learning resources, while the one-group design limits causal interpretation. Continued refinement, responsible AI-use guidance, and testing in additional instructional settings are recommended.

items.title: Development of a KYTC Highway Geometric Design Workshop
items.abstract: In-depth knowledge of geometric design principles is a prerequisite for delivering road projects that provide safe and efficient multimodal mobility for all users. Historically, Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) early-career design staff arrived at the agency with little design experience. The agency has relied on a combination of short courses and mentorship provided by experienced personnel to bring early-career design staff up to speed on design best practices. However, this approach to training carries limitations. Employee turnover and imposing workloads make it challenging for early- and even mid-career design professionals to receive guidance from seasoned designers who have long tenures at KYTC. And it hinders efforts to implement a consistent design philosophy across the agency. Recognizing that young designers, as well as project managers and project reviewers, would benefit from a course focused on geometric design, Kentucky Transportation Center (KTC) researchers worked with Cabinet staff to develop and deliver the Roadway Geometry Fundamentals Course. This five-day training introduces participants to a mix of foundational concepts (e.g., horizontal and vertical alignment, sight distance, cross-sectional elements, speed management, intersection design, roadside safety) and advanced topics (e.g., innovative design, context classification, human factors). The course blends instructor-led lectures, group exercises, and discussion to achieve learning objectives. A pilot version of the course was delivered in October 2025, and multiple offerings are planned for 2026. Long term, KYTC views the Roadway Geometry Fundamentals Course as an important vehicle for achieving agencywide consistency in design practice and elevating Kentucky to a position of national leadership in innovative design and road safety.

items.title: Effects of AI-mediated real-time feedback on motivation and motor skill learning in traditional ethnic sports education: testing self-determination theory mechanisms
items.abstract: Introduction Traditional ethnic sports such as Zhuang Daoyin demand precise movement, yet conventional demonstration–imitation–verbal correction limits feedback timeliness and individualization. Artificial intelligence (AI) real-time posture feedback offers a scalable option, but most evaluations emphasize technical outcomes and overlook learning processes. Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study tested whether and how AI real-time feedback improves motivation and motor skill by engaging basic psychological needs, with competence as the hypothesized pathway. Methods In a 12-week field experiment, 12 intact classes (307 students; control n = 152, AI n = 155) were randomly allocated at the class level to an AI real-time feedback group or a traditional teaching group; three instructors each taught two classes per condition. Both groups received identical instruction; conditions differed only in feedback source during practice (RTMPose-based concurrent vs. teacher-led terminal feedback). Need satisfaction, motivational regulation (relative autonomy index, RAI), motor skill, and course satisfaction were assessed at pre- and post-test, and analyzed with linear mixed models and structural equation modeling (lavaan, MLR). Results The AI group showed significantly greater gains in competence ( d = 0.36, p = 0.003), autonomy ( d = 0.40, p = 0.001), motor skill ( d = 0.30, p = 0.010), and learning interest ( d = 0.38, p = 0.003), whereas relatedness was unaffected ( p = 0.974); intraclass correlations were negligible. In the structural model (CFI = 0.94, RMSEA = 0.04, SRMR = 0.04), group predicted competence ( β = 0.17), competence predicted RAI ( β = 0.34), and RAI predicted motor skill ( β = 0.30); the autonomy and relatedness paths were nonsignificant. The effect of AI feedback on motor skill was fully mediated by the competence-to-RAI sequence (indirect p = 0.023; direct p = 0.097). Discussion AI real-time feedback improved motor skill by strengthening competence and supporting motivational internalization, while leaving relatedness unaffected—providing discriminant evidence that the tool acts through its affordances rather than diffuse enthusiasm. Systems enhancing performance and learning should prioritize feedback that makes progress legible, within a human–AI division of labor where teachers provide relational support. In conclusion, AI real-time posture feedback can enhance motivation and motor skill learning by satisfying learners’ competence need.

items.title: Emerging Technology-Supported Intercultural Learning for Cognitive, Attitudinal, and Behavioral Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Three-Level Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Emerging technologies are increasingly used to support intercultural learning, yet evidence on the distinct effects of artificial intelligence (AI), augmented reality (AR), and virtual reality (VR) remains limited. This systematic review and three-level meta-analysis synthesized 17 studies published from 2020 to July 2026 (77 effect sizes) to examine cognitive, attitudinal, and behavioral outcomes. The overall effect was large and significant (Hedges’ g = 0.965, 95% CI [0.580, 1.350], p < .001), although heterogeneity was substantial. AI-supported interventions also showed a significant positive pooled effect (g = 1.150, 95% CI [0.744, 1.555], p < .001). AR showed a significantly larger estimated effect than VR (β = −1.481 for VR relative to AR, p = .017), but this difference was not robust to excluding one AR study. Academic level (F (1, 75) = 17.27, p < .001) and sample size (F (2, 74) = 3.873, p = .026) were significant moderators, with larger effects in K–12 and larger-sample studies. However, these exploratory comparisons involved uneven technology distributions and only two K–12 studies. Outcome domain did not significantly moderate effects. Sensitivity analyses supported the stability of the overall pooled effect. The findings indicate that emerging technologies can improve intercultural learning, while better-balanced comparative studies are needed to identify which technological approaches are most effective.

items.title: Employee responses to workplace AI across cultural contexts: a systematic review of explicitly AI-framed evidence
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI and large language models is reshaping how work is organised and how employees engage with emerging technologies. Yet the role of culture in these responses remains poorly understood and is often inferred from contextual proxies rather than measured directly. This systematic review synthesises empirical journal studies of explicitly AI-framed technologies in workplace and professional settings, with particular attention to directly measured cultural values and culturally situated conditions. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO via EBSCOhost and PubMed identified 910 records. A complete re-screening during revision of an updated title-distinct set of 691 records yielded 13 eligible studies. The evidence base was small, heterogeneous and methodologically uneven. Only four studies directly examined named cultural-value constructs, while the remainder represented culture through national context, organisational culture, professional culture or locally grounded frameworks. Across studies, employee responses ranged from acceptance, trust and optimism to uncertainty, perceived threat, autonomy, professional identity, human–AI collaboration, innovation, job crafting and adaptation. Rather than indicating a consistent cultural effect, the findings suggest that cultural influences are contingent on how culture is operationalised and on the organisational and professional settings in which AI is introduced. Stronger multilevel designs, more direct measurement of cultural values and clearer separation of cultural, national and organisational influences are needed before robust cross-cultural conclusions can be drawn.

items.title: Enterprise Agentic AI Reference Architecture
items.abstract: Agentic AI extends Generative AI from response generation to goal-oriented digital execution. Enterprise agents can interpret objectives, plan tasks, retrieve knowledge, invoke tools, call APIs, maintain memory, coordinate with other agents, and adapt execution based on intermediate results. These capabilities require a reference architecture that separates probabilistic reasoning from deterministic enterprise controls. This paper proposes an Enterprise Agentic AI Reference Architecture spanning experience, agent orchestration, planning and reasoning, enterprise knowledge, memory, model runtime, tool and integration services, identity, policy enforcement, observability, security, Responsible AI, and human oversight. The architecture integrates SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP HANA Cloud, SAP Integration Suite, enterprise APIs, RAG, Knowledge Graphs, and cloud-native services. It provides patterns for secure and scalable agent deployment across hybrid and multi-cloud environments while preserving accountability, bounded autonomy, operational resilience, and business value.

items.title: Enterprise AI Trust, Risk and Compliance (AI TRiSM) Framework
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is becoming embedded in enterprise decisions, customer interactions, software engineering, operations, and autonomous workflows. As adoption expands, organizations must manage not only model performance but also trust, risk, security, compliance, explainability, privacy, resilience, and accountability. This paper proposes an Enterprise AI Trust, Risk and Compliance (AI TRiSM) Framework that integrates enterprise architecture, AI governance, model risk management, cybersecurity, privacy, Responsible AI, legal compliance, observability, and lifecycle controls. The framework establishes governance domains for AI inventory, risk classification, model assurance, data and prompt governance, identity, security, human oversight, monitoring, incident response, regulatory evidence, and recertification. It supports predictive AI, Generative AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Agentic AI across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. The proposed approach enables enterprises to scale AI while maintaining measurable trust, bounded risk, defensible compliance, and clear accountability.

items.title: Enterprise Architecture for Autonomous Enterprises
items.abstract: Autonomous enterprises increasingly combine Artificial Intelligence, Agentic AI, automation, event-driven platforms, digital twins, data products, and intelligent decision services to execute business processes with reduced manual intervention. Traditional enterprise architecture methods are often insufficient when systems can plan, reason, act, learn, and coordinate dynamically across organizational boundaries. This paper proposes an Enterprise Architecture for Autonomous Enterprises framework that aligns business capabilities, operating models, data, applications, integration, AI, security, governance, and human oversight. The framework introduces architectural principles for bounded autonomy, policy-driven execution, decision rights, digital workforce governance, real-time observability, resilience, and continuous assurance. It also defines reference layers, implementation stages, governance gates, and measurable outcomes. The proposed approach enables organizations to scale autonomous operations while maintaining accountability, interoperability, trust, regulatory readiness, and business control.

items.abstract: Enterprises are rapidly moving from isolated copilots toward ecosystems of specialized AI agents that collaborate across business processes, data domains, applications, and cloud platforms. This paper proposes an Enterprise Multi-Agent Architecture Framework that defines a layered architecture for agent discovery, orchestration, inter-agent communication, knowledge grounding, enterprise integration, policy enforcement, runtime isolation, and human oversight. The framework combines enterprise architecture principles, Zero Trust, Responsible AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graphs, API governance, event-driven integration, and lifecycle management. It enables organizations to design scalable multi-agent environments in which specialized agents can collaborate safely while maintaining traceability, bounded authority, data protection, and measurable business outcomes across hybrid and multi-cloud landscapes.

items.title: Equipping the next generation: addressing the unmet need for artificial intelligence education at research performing organizations
items.abstract: Abstract Background The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools into higher education is rapidly accelerating, yet the educational ecosystem appears largely unprepared for the scale and speed of adoption. Our recent international survey of over 1,200 university students and postdoctoral fellows in the medical and life sciences found that while more than 80% had used GenAI tools, the vast majority had received no formal training, and many were unaware of any institutional policies governing their use. This gap between adoption and institutional preparedness may pose risks to research integrity if left unaddressed. Main body Existing research supports a coordinated, evidence-informed approach to AI education in research performing organizations (RPOs), grounded in principles of research integrity, equity, and critical engagement with technology. First, GenAI literacy must be embedded as a core competency in scientific and clinical education, equipping students to critically evaluate tool outputs, recognize hallucination and bias, and understand the distinction between AI-generated inaccuracy and deliberate research misconduct. Second, traditional frameworks for academic integrity would benefit from re-examination. Today, GenAI tools have fundamentally disrupted established notions of authorship, originality, and plagiarism, and the absence of coherent institutional guidance leaves students and educators navigating these questions without support. Third, RPOs must develop clear, transparent, and context-sensitive policies on GenAI use by embedding responsible AI education into curricula, equipping learners not only to use these tools effectively, but to question, verify, and critique their outputs in ways that uphold scientific standards. Conclusion RPOs have an urgent responsibility to move beyond reactive responses and toward proactive strategies that uphold scientific standards, promote equity of access, and prepare the next generation of researchers and clinicians to engage with GenAI responsibly and ethically.

Parental support, benefits (psychological, physical and social) and the pursuit of health lead to sports practice according to athletes’ reports. items.title: Ethical leadership and job crafting: the role of intrinsic motivation and job feedback
items.abstract: Introduction Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and its sub-theory Cognitive Evaluation Theory (CET), the present study examines how ethical leadership relates to employees’ job crafting through intrinsic motivation, and how this indirect relationship is contingent on job feedback. We proposed that ethical leadership is positively related to job crafting via intrinsic motivation, and that job feedback moderates this indirect effect by providing competence-relevant informational cues. Methods We tested our hypotheses using two-wave data collected from 102 employees in the customer service department of a gaming company in northern China. Results The results provided preliminary evidence of a moderated mediation pattern, suggesting that the indirect association between ethical leadership and job crafting through intrinsic motivation varied as a function of job feedback. Discussion These findings extend research on ethical leadership and job crafting by clarifying intrinsic motivation as the motivational mechanism and job feedback as a key boundary condition. The theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

items.title: Ethics of AI and Non-Human Entities
items.abstract: This paper examines the ethical and philosophical implications of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology—not for human society, but for “non-human beings” and the Earth’s ecosystems.Conventional discussions of AI ethics and the philosophy of technology have consistently remained within an “anthropocentric” framework focused on human labor, copyright, or whether AI possesses a mind equivalent to that of humans.However, modern AI is already deeply penetrating the natural world.In this paper, from the perspectives of environmental philosophy and bioethics, we present three core paradigms: I) the redefinition of the dignity of life brought about by the translation of animal language using AI; II) signal pollution in the natural world caused by digital technology (ecological deepfakes); and III) the environmental burden and infringement on the right to life of other organisms resulting from the materiality of computation.In conclusion, we argue that future AI ethics must undergo a paradigm shift toward “Environmental AI Ethics,” which encompasses all life systems beyond humans. items.title: Factors associated with generative AI chatbot acceptance among medical students with prior academic use: a cross-sectional study based on an extended technology acceptance model
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are becoming increasingly embedded in medical education, providing students with on-demand support for learning, clinical reasoning, and academic tasks. However, the psychological and technological factors that shape medical students’ acceptance of these tools remain insufficiently understood. This study examined acceptance among medical students with prior academic use of GenAI chatbots by extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to include AI literacy (AIL) and perceived security and privacy (PSP), and by examining their associations with perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), attitude toward using GenAI (ATG), and behavioral intention to use GenAI (BIG). A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among medical students at Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences (HUMS), Iran, between May and June 2026. Eligibility required prior academic use of a GenAI chatbot. Data were collected using a structured, self-administered questionnaire and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model was assessed for reliability and validity, while the structural model was evaluated using path coefficients (β), coefficients of determination ( R ²), and effect sizes ( f ²). Of the 292 students invited, 267 completed the survey, and 252 participants with prior academic use of GenAI chatbots were included in the final analysis (mean age, 22.64 ± 2.28 years; 147 [58.3%] female). The measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and validity. AIL was positively associated with PEOU (β = 0.479, p < 0.001), while PSP was positively associated with PU (β = 0.157, p = 0.005). PEOU and PU were positively associated with ATG, and ATG showed the strongest association with BIG (β = 0.524, p < 0.001). The model explained 38.7% of the variance in BIG, with R ² values ranging from 0.229 to 0.387 across the endogenous constructs. The findings indicate that medical students’ acceptance of GenAI chatbots is associated with AIL and PSP alongside the core TAM constructs of PEOU and PU, with ATG showing the strongest association with BIG. Strengthening AIL and establishing clear privacy and security policies may support the informed and responsible integration of GenAI chatbots into medical education.

items.title: From Anthropomorphism to Trust: Unpacking the Role of Authenticity in Generative AI and Large Language Models—A Structured Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has changed the conditions under which users encounter and evaluate machine-produced communication. In systems based on large language models, conversational output is no longer merely functional; it can be fluent, context-aware, and socially legible, inviting judgments that extend beyond usefulness, accuracy, or efficiency. Yet the literature still tends to treat anthropomorphism, perceived authenticity, and trust as largely separate constructs, without sufficiently explaining how human-like cues become credible in the eyes of users and how this credibility shapes trust. To address this problem, the present structured literature review synthesizes recent research on anthropomorphism, authenticity-related evaluations, and trust in AI-mediated interaction, with particular attention to conversational AI, generative AI, and LLM-based systems. A structured search in the Web of Science Core Collection identified 655 records; after duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, 96 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The analysis identifies several interrelated thematic patterns, including anthropomorphic cues and social presence, authenticity-related mechanisms in AI-mediated communication, trust formation and calibration, boundary conditions, and behavioral responses to conversational AI. On this basis, the review develops an integrative conceptual framework and proposes perceived anthropomorphic authenticity as a review-derived construct for examining how users evaluate human-like AI communication in relation to trust. The study contributes to human–AI interaction research by clarifying the role of authenticity-related evaluations between anthropomorphic cues and calibrated trust and by identifying conditions under which human-like communication may be associated with trust, skepticism, overreliance, or trust erosion.

items.title: From Permitted Actions to Trusted Outcomes
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can read sensitive information, execute privileged commands, and move data betweenenterprise systems. Existing authentication and authorization checks remain necessary, but a tool call can be permittedwhile the sequence of calls produces a result outside the authorized business task. This paper addresses a practicalsecurity problem: how can an enterprise detect and stop a harmful sequence of individually permitted actions beforea damaging action executes? It proposes Trajectory-Aware Zero Trust (TA-ZT), a vendor-neutral referencearchitecture that combines DoD Zero Trust pillars, CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2, task-scoped authorization,action history, data lineage, and independent policy enforcement. items.abstract: In this literature narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies for colorectal endoscopy (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library, January 2015 to June 2026, with supplementary hand-searching), the "pixels-to-prevention" paradigm -image interpretation → detection → characterization → clinical decision → treatment quality → surveillance → prevention -is employed to examine whether the well-evidenced performance characteristics of AI can actually be tied to effective cancer prevention rather than merely listing out the different types of applications of AI that were reported in previous reviews.Colorectal cancer prevention is strongly connected to colonoscopy but is limited by lesion miss rates, endoscopist variability, and interpretation of the results into management.Computer-aided detection enhances the adenoma detection rates and reduces the lesion miss rate, but the higher adenoma detection rates is just a surrogate and does not directly contribute to cancer prevention: AI-assisted colonoscopy prefers the detection of diminutive and non-neoplastic lesions rather than advanced neoplasms.This review traces the evolution from computer-aided detection to computer-aided characterization and optical diagnosis, highlighting their recent applications for quality control of resection, prediction of recurrence development, and individualized surveillance based on risk stratification where we distinguish advances in metrics of performance from clinical utility (interval colorectal cancer, unneeded resections, surveillance burden).The review considers the questions related to the problem of false positives, algorithm bias, dataset variability, lack of external validation, automation bias, interpretability, workflow, and regulation.Asking ourselves how intelligent endoscopy could help us going beyond the discovery of lesions through the use of artificial intelligence, we propose an agenda for research that focuses on validation and patient outcome.

items.title: From Rules to Autonomous Agents: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Human-AI Integration, and the Governance of Agentic Systems-A Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved from rule-based symbolic systems into learning architectures capable of perception, prediction, content generation, reasoning, planning, tool use, and increasingly autonomous action. This qualitative literature review examines this transition as more than a technological chronology. It interprets AI evolution through five interrelated dimensions: technological evolution, capability expansion, changing human roles, human–AI integration, and governance. Drawing on contemporary peer-reviewed literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026, the review identifies seven thematic developments. AI has progressed from encoded rules toward learned representations and goal-directed action; generative AI has expanded AI into a general-purpose content collaborator; agentic AI adds planning, memory, tool use, and iterative task execution; human roles increasingly shift from operator toward collaborator, delegator, and governor; human–AI complementarity remains conditional rather than automatic; effective deployment requires calibrated rather than maximal trust; and governance requirements increase as AI systems acquire greater operational agency. The article proposes the Evolution–Capability–Role–Integration–Governance (ECRIG) framework to explain these relationships. The framework suggests that sustainable benefits from advanced AI emerge when technological capability, human role allocation, interaction architecture, and governance mechanisms develop jointly. The review concludes that the central challenge of the agentic-AI era is not choosing between humans and machines, but designing accountable systems in which increasingly capable artificial agents remain aligned with meaningful human goals, authority, and oversight.

items.title: Functional profile and work demands-capacity matching as tools for assessing the risk of continued employment among workers 55 years and older
items.abstract: Population ageing in the workforce is one of the key challenges for contemporary labour markets. This article aims to present and critically evaluate a conceptual model for assessing the risk of reduced or discontinued employment among individuals aged ≥55 years. The study is a review based on an integrative synthesis of literature on work ability, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, job crafting, work design, and research on retention and return to work. The proposed model is based on an employee functional profile and a task-matching matrix. It assumes task-level analysis of work, with tasks assessed in terms of physical, cognitive, emotional, and social demands, as well as organizational and personal value. Based on this, 4 types of organizational decisions are identified: task maintenance, workload reduction, task redistribution, and task enrichment. The model enables the identification of risk configurations, such as accumulation of demands, erosion of work value, impaired recovery, environmental mismatch, and underuse of competences. However, it is not a validated predictive tool. The proposed framework supports the design of work that promotes longer, healthier, and more sustainable working lives among workers aged ≥55 years. Further empirical validation and sector-specific adaptation are required. Med Pr Work Health Saf. 2026;77(5).
